title: Stripe Uses Graph Search and State Machines to Automate Database Remediation
gist: Stripe replaced hard-coded, plugin-based database remediation with a model of its MongoDB fleet as a graph, using Dijkstra-based pathfinding plus state machines to compute and execute recovery plans that adapt to any shard layout. The result is roughly 30% fewer database pager alerts — about 200 fewer pages a year and 12 days of unhealthy shard states eliminated — against a prior baseline of 124 pages in six months for misconfigured shards alone, and the team argues a state machine discovers novel recovery procedures that runbooks cannot encode.

insights.claim: Stripe's original hard-coded, plugin-based database remediation system did not scale because of fragile dependencies, complex multi-failure scenarios, layout-specific logic and unhandled intermediate states that repeatedly forced manual intervention.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Rule-per-scenario automation degrades combinatorially at fleet scale — a warning for anyone buying runbook-automation tools priced per playbook.
insights.locator: Stripe found that its original hard-coded, plugin-based remediation system

insights.claim: In one six-month window Stripe's control plane paged operators 124 times for misconfigured shards and 32 times for single-node-down scenarios complicated by additional health issues.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A concrete baseline for the human cost of database fleet operations at a large payments company, useful for sizing similar toil elsewhere.
insights.quote: In one six-month window, the control plane paged operators 124 times for misconfigured shards, and 32 times for single-node-down scenarios complicated by additional health issues.

insights.claim: Critical operations such as index builds and planned maintenance were blocked for an average of one hour per incident under the old remediation system.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Unhealthy-state blocking has a direct throughput cost on scheduled work, not just an alerting cost — the fuller ROI case for automation.
insights.locator: Critical operations like index builds and planned maintenance were blocked

insights.claim: Stripe models its MongoDB infrastructure as a graph where nodes represent infrastructure components, edges capture relationships and node attributes describe current state, turning recovery into a pathfinding problem.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A reusable architectural pattern for self-healing infrastructure that generalizes beyond databases to any stateful fleet.
insights.locator: Stripe addressed these limitations by modeling its MongoDB infrastructure as a graph

insights.claim: By removing fixed remediation sequences in favor of graph traversal to identify valid recovery paths, the same remediation logic adapts automatically to different database layouts and evolving infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Layout-agnostic remediation removes the maintenance tax that normally makes automation decay as infrastructure changes.
insights.locator: Removing the previous hard-coded remediation sequences

insights.claim: Stripe started with breadth-first search for valid remediation paths but moved to Dijkstra's algorithm to prioritize lower-cost recovery plans, cutting unnecessary operations while preserving correctness.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Cost-weighted pathfinding is the detail that makes automated remediation safe to run unattended — the difference between a valid plan and a cheap one.
insights.locator: Stripe initially used breadth first search (BFS)

insights.claim: Because Dijkstra's algorithm explores paths to all reachable states rather than only the goal state, Stripe gets partial remediation: when no complete path exists the system moves the fleet to the least misconfigured state.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Graceful degradation toward the least-bad reachable state is a design property most incident automation lacks and a strong argument for the graph approach.
insights.quote: Because Dijkstra's algorithm explores paths to all reachable states rather than only the goal state, we can also get partial remediation. When no complete path exists, the algorithm returns the path to the least misconfigured state.
insights.locator: Stripe initially used breadth first search (BFS), but later adopted Dijkstra's algorithm

insights.claim: Stripe models remediation as composable rules with explicit state transitions rather than embedding recovery logic in fixed workflows, letting the planner combine operations dynamically as infrastructure evolves.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Composability is what allows one planner to cover combinatorial failure modes without a linear increase in engineering effort.
insights.locator: Rather than embedding recovery logic in fixed workflows

insights.claim: The graph-based system dynamically adapts to different MongoDB shard layouts and has reduced database-related pager alerts by about 30%.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A quantified 30% alert reduction sets a benchmark for evaluating self-healing infrastructure claims from vendors.
insights.locator: According to the authors, the system now dynamically adapts

insights.claim: The alert reduction translates to 200 fewer pages per year and eliminates an estimated 12 days of unhealthy shard states annually.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Twelve days of unhealthy state removed is a reliability improvement, not just a quality-of-life one — it shrinks the window where a second failure becomes an outage.
insights.locator: This translates to 200 fewer pages per year

insights.claim: Stripe plans to extend the framework beyond failure recovery to automate topology changes and blue-green deployments and to orchestrate planned maintenance alongside reactive healing.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: The same planner covering both proactive change and reactive healing collapses two toolchains into one — the direction infrastructure automation is heading.
insights.locator: the team plans to extend the framework beyond failure recovery

insights.claim: Stripe argues that state machine modeling, simulation-based planning and runtime pathfinding are a compelling alternative to accumulating ever-more-specific runbooks, because runbooks encode known recovery procedures while a state machine discovers novel ones.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: This is a direct challenge to the runbook-automation and AI-runbook product category: search over a state model generalizes where documented procedures cannot.
insights.quote: Runbooks encode known recovery procedures; a state machine discovers novel ones.

insights.claim: At global database fleet scale, hardware degradation and unhealthy shards are daily occurrences, so the real challenge is fixing them without burning out on-call engineers, per Stripe's head of developer infrastructure Scott MacVicar.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Operator burnout, not technical failure, is framed as the binding constraint at fleet scale — the human-cost argument that funds this class of automation.
insights.quote: At scale, the challenge isn't just fixing issues. It is doing so without burning out your on-call engineers.
insights.locator: Scott MacVicar, head of developer infrastructure at Stripe, writes on LinkedIn

insights.claim: Stripe is not alone in investing in automated infrastructure operations: Uber has described its declarative, self-healing Odin platform and Meta has detailed AI-assisted tooling to accelerate incident response.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Self-healing infrastructure is converging across large operators, which usually precedes the pattern being productized and sold to the mid-market.
insights.locator: Stripe is not the only large software company investing
